- Use @ instead of & for reference sigil

1. Content-addressed definitions — kill the file, kill the name-as-identity.

A function's true identity is the hash of its content, not its name or location. Names become local aliases you can change for free. Prior art: Unison, and it's the most underrated idea in language design. The revolution is what falls out of it: renaming is instant and global with zero risk; there are no merge conflicts on unrelated code because unrelated code has different hashes; "dependency hell" disappears because old code still resolves to the exact bytes it always did. Psychology: it kills naming anxiety (names stop being permanent global commitments) and loss aversion (you literally cannot break a downstream consumer—the old hash is immutable).

5. Effects/capabilities so a signature tells you everything a function can do.

If a function isn't granted network or filesystem capability, it provably cannot touch them—visible right in the signature. Prior art: Koka, Unison's "abilities," Eff, Frank, and capability-based security research. Still wildly niche in practice. Value prop: you can trust a dependency by reading its type instead of auditing its source. This is the foundation for a supply-chain-attack-resistant ecosystem.

7. Uncertainty as a pervasive type dimension.

Not just probabilistic programming (Stan, Church, Pyro do statistics). I mean a tracked axis on ordinary values: "this might be null," "this came from untrusted user input," "this data is possibly stale," "this is an estimate ±5%." The type system propagates the uncertainty and forces you to discharge it before it can cause harm. Value prop: the entire category of "I assumed this was fresh/clean/present" bugs becomes a type error.

8. Negative-space types — declare what code must never do.

Every language lets you say what code does; almost none let you say what it's forbidden from doing ("this module may never allocate," "this path may never log PII," "this loop may never block"). First-class prohibitions, statically enforced. Psychology: humans reason about safety in terms of guarantees and red lines, not just behaviors. This matches how engineers actually think about risk.

9. Cost/resource types.

The type tracks computational cost—time complexity, allocation, energy, latency budget. Prior art is fringe (some research languages, and Granule for resource semantics). Value prop: "this function is O(n²)" or "this handler exceeds its 10ms budget" becomes a compile error, not a 2 a.m. production incident. Increasingly urgent for embedded, real-time, and energy-conscious computing.

10. Reactive/dataflow-by-default — the whole program is a spreadsheet. **Consider this as tooling**

State synchronization is one of the largest sources of bugs and one of the most exhausting things to hold in your head. Make automatic recalculation the core model, not a framework you bolt on. Prior art: Eve, FRP, and the fact that spreadsheets are the most successful programming environment in history and almost no general-purpose language learned from them. Psychology: removes the entire cognitive burden of "did I remember to update everything downstream?"

12. Maturity/confidence tiers in the type system.

Code is tagged experimental, tested, or battle-hardened, and the compiler forbids battle-hardened code from silently depending on experimental code. You're encoding the social reality of a codebase into the language itself. Psychology: this matches the actual mental model every senior engineer carries informally ("don't build on that, it's a prototype") and makes it enforceable instead of tribal knowledge.
